title: Normalizing NVIDIA Vera Benchmarks to AMD EPYC Turin A Framework
gist: ServeTheHome deconstructs NVIDIA's Vera CPU whitepaper, showing that its headline 12.7GB/s vs 3.1GB/s per-core memory bandwidth gap is largely a denominator choice (88 Vera cores vs 128 EPYC 9755 cores, a 45% larger divisor) layered on a two-year memory vintage gap that AMD's 1.6TB/s Venice will close. It also shows NVIDIA's monolithic core-to-core latency advantage holds only through 88 cores and inverts beyond that into socket-to-socket and then PCIe/NIC/switch hops, and supplies SMT conversion factors (core+SMT = 1.3x, single thread = 0.65x) for reading per-thread claims.

insights.claim: NVIDIA published its Vera CPU whitepaper with the first SPEC CPU 2026 benchmarks just before AMD's Advancing AI 2026 event, a timing choice that lets a vendor compare against the outgoing generation rather than the concurrent one.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A reusable tell for reading vendor benchmark releases: launch-window timing determines which competitor generation appears in the charts.
insights.quote: Companies typically do this because the valid comparison is versus the outgoing generation rather than the concurrent generation.
insights.locator: 'Normalizing the NVIDIA Vera Whitepaper Numbers to AMD EPYC Turin'

insights.claim: NVIDIA Vera is an Arm-compatible server CPU built on custom Olympus cores, with 88 cores per socket in the published comparison.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Establishes the concrete competitive object: a custom-core Arm server CPU from NVIDIA aimed squarely at AMD's x86 server franchise.
insights.quote: NVIDIA Vera appears to be an interesting Arm-compatible server CPU with its custom Olympus cores

insights.claim: Every vendor crafts favorable comparisons, so readers should build their own normalized framework rather than accept the published ratio.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The central editorial stance — treat first-party silicon benchmark ratios as marketing artifacts until re-normalized on cores, sockets and memory vintage.
insights.quote: Like virtually every company that produces products, NVIDIA crafted favorable comparisons.

insights.claim: Memory bandwidth is mostly channels multiplied by channel speed, so a large part of any bandwidth comparison between CPUs from different years is really a comparison of memory vintages rather than architectures.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Deflates bandwidth-led marketing claims — the metric tracks the memory calendar, so leadership flips with each generation regardless of core design.
insights.quote: That means a large portion of any bandwidth comparison between CPUs from different years is really a comparison of memory vintages.
insights.locator: 'Socket memory bandwidth and per-core memory bandwidth'

insights.claim: Twelve channels of DDR5-6400 on the 2024-era AMD EPYC 9755 deliver roughly 0.6TB/s of peak bandwidth, NVIDIA Vera's LPDDR5X-9600 reaches up to 1.2TB/s, and AMD has already stated that Venice will deliver 1.6TB/s with 16-channel systems already shown.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The bandwidth ladder implies Vera's memory advantage is a one-generation window that closes when Venice ships — a timing risk for anyone extrapolating Vera leadership.
insights.quote: Twelve channels of DDR5-6400 on the 2024-era EPYC 9755 deliver roughly 0.6TB/s of peak bandwidth. Vera’s LPDDR5X-9600 is up to 1.2TB/s. AMD has already said Venice is 1.6TB/s of memory bandwidth
insights.locator: 'Socket memory bandwidth and per-core memory bandwidth'

insights.claim: NVIDIA's headline per-core memory bandwidth figure of 12.7GB/s versus 3.1GB/s is inflated by dividing AMD's older, slower memory by the 128 cores of the EPYC 9755 while dividing its own newer memory by 88 cores — a denominator 45% larger on AMD's side.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Shows exactly how a 4x headline ratio is manufactured; a 96-core EPYC 9655 comparison would compress the gap materially.
insights.quote: NVIDIA is using a 45% larger denominator on AMD’s side than on its own Vera CPU.
insights.locator: 'The whitepaper’s memory bandwidth per core figure'

insights.claim: AMD produced a comparably dramatic bandwidth chart itself when moving from EPYC 7003 Milan (8-channel DDR4-3200) to EPYC 9004 Genoa (12-channel DDR5-4800), so once the 128-core denominator is changed to 88 or 96 the Vera-versus-Turin chart looks much like a Milan-to-Genoa transition.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Reframes Vera's memory story as a normal generational step rather than an architectural breakthrough — important for sizing NVIDIA's actual CPU threat to AMD.
insights.quote: Once you change the 128-core denominator to 88 or 96, the chart looks a lot more like a Milan-to-Genoa route.
insights.locator: 'AMD EPYC 9004 Genoa DDR5 Memory Capabilities Bandwidth'

insights.claim: NVIDIA's core-to-core latency heat map showing AMD mostly red outside CCX and CCD structures and Vera mostly green is directionally accurate, because chiplets add hops and hops add latency.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Concedes a real monolithic-die advantage — but only in the range where the topology claim actually holds.
insights.quote: Chiplets add hops, and hops add latency.

insights.claim: Agentic workloads generally run in VMs, containers or sandboxes using 1-4 cores each, which fit entirely within a single EPYC CCX when the OS schedules them properly, so those workloads live in the green cells of AMD's own chart and a single-core sandbox is barely exposed to core-to-core latency at all.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Undercuts the core-to-core latency attack for the exact workload class NVIDIA is targeting — the strongest counter to Vera's topology marketing.
insights.quote: A workload that stays inside a CCX lives in the green cells of AMD’s own chart, and a single core sandbox is barely exposed to core-to-core latency at all.

insights.claim: Vera's monolithic latency advantage inverts beyond 88 cores: a like-for-like 128-core test would require cores 89 through 128 to come from a second socket, crossing socket-to-socket links with much higher latency and jitter than an on-package chiplet hop.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The decisive normalization point — at the very core counts NVIDIA chose for its comparison, its own topology argument reverses.
insights.quote: The monolithic latency story holds through 88 cores and inverts beyond them.
insights.locator: 'The conveniently incomplete part of the story'

insights.claim: Beyond 176 cores the Vera hop is no longer even within a node: cores 177 to 256 sit behind a PCIe hop to a NIC, a NIC hop to a switch, a switch hop to a NIC, then a PCIe hop to another CPU.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Quantifies where per-socket core count actually matters — dense x86 sockets avoid network hops that no monolithic die can eliminate.
insights.quote: Cores 177 to 256 are now a PCIe hop to a NIC, a NIC hop to a switch, a switch hop to a NIC, then a PCIe hop to a CPU away.

insights.claim: There is a legitimate Vera advantage in poorly tuned environments where a scheduler fragments a 4-core workload across the CPU, because a large monolithic die is the safer topology in that case.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: The honest steelman: NVIDIA's topology wins where software tuning is weak, which is common in enterprise rather than hyperscale deployments.
insights.quote: It is true that if a scheduler fragments a 4-core workload by placing threads across the CPU, a large, monolithic die is a safer topology.

insights.claim: When a vendor publishes single-thread versus single-core results for an SMT-capable CPU the terms are used deliberately and differ: a single-threaded EPYC result is one hardware thread of two, while a single-core result includes both threads.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A specific way non-SMT vendors gain an apparent per-unit advantage — check which denominator underlies any single-thread claim.
insights.quote: A single-threaded result on an EPYC part is one hardware thread of two

insights.claim: In ServeTheHome's testing, loading the second SMT thread adds roughly 12% on a Skylake-era Xeon with default side-channel mitigations, 23-25% on Sapphire Rapids, 29-32% on Xeon 6 and 32-33% on Zen 5, with Zen 5c a few points lower because it hits L3 cache misses more often.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Hard multipliers for converting per-thread benchmark claims into per-core reality across the last four server CPU generations.
insights.quote: loading the second thread adds roughly 12% on a Skylake-era Xeon (with default side channel mitigations active), 23-25% on Sapphire Rapids, 29-32% on Xeon 6, and 32-33% on Zen 5

insights.claim: On modern SMT implementations, if one core is 1.0 then one core with its SMT thread is 1.3 and one thread alone is 0.65, which is why non-SMT vendors have historically preferred the per-thread metric.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: A one-line conversion factor that neutralizes per-thread framing — directly applicable as Arm server CPUs without SMT proliferate.
insights.quote: So if one core is 1.0, one core with its SMT thread is 1.3, and one thread is 0.65.

insights.claim: ServeTheHome discloses it works with both AMD and NVIDIA, remains under embargo on AMD's Venice, and published a more extensive version of this analysis on its paid Substack for a different audience first.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Context for weighting the analysis: the author has commercial relationships with both vendors and is withholding Venice data under embargo.
insights.quote: A few quick disclosures that we work with both AMD and NVIDIA.
